mainTopic: Two cases where a person admits privately to the judge that his document is forged, but says he once had a real one that got lost. רבה wants to believe him because he could have lied better (מה לו לשקר), and רב יוסף objects that a forged document is worthless.
overview: This amud finishes a story about a man living on a field who showed a bill of sale. The original owner said it was forged, and the man quietly admitted it to רבה but said he once had a real one that got lost. רבה believes him, since he could have just said the document was real (מה לו לשקר). רב יוסף objects that a forged document is worthless and gives nothing to rely on. The same argument repeats in a matching case about a loan document. רב אידי בר אבין rules: follow רבה for land and רב יוסף for money, so in both cases things stay where they are. אביי then uses that rule to decide a guarantor's claim, and the גמרא limits it: coins handed back because they were worn or discolored never counted as payment, so the document still works. Finally, a rumor spreads that רבא בר שרשום is profiting from orphans' land. When אביי asks what happened, he begins explaining that he held it as a משכנתא from their father, and his explanation continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The owner says the bill of sale is forged, and the holder quietly admits it
steps.stepSummary: The original owner claims the bill of sale is forged. The man on the land whispers to רבה that it is forged, but says he once had a real one that got lost.
steps.simpleTranslation: The original owner said: 'This document is forged!' The man on the land leaned over and whispered to רבה: 'Yes, it is forged. But I really had a proper bill of sale, and it got lost. So I thought I would at least hold on to this one, whatever it is worth.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes setting up the case: the man on the land admits, only to the judge, that his document is fake but says he once had a real one. This sets up רבה's ruling in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man on the land is not simply denying the forgery. He agrees with the other side that the paper is fake, but adds a new claim: he truly bought the field and lost the real document. The question now is whether to believe that private claim.

keyTerms.meaning: Whatever it is worth; at least something

steps.confusionAlert: He whispers his admission only to the judge, not out loud to the other side. In front of the other side, his claim stays the same: the field is his.

phrases.english: He said to him: It is a forged document!
phrases.notes: This is the original owner answering the man who is living on the field and showed a bill of sale.

phrases.english: He leaned over and whispered to Rabba:
Yes, it is a forged document;
but I had a proper document,
and it got lost, and I said to myself:
I will hold this one in my hand, whatever it is worth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the case from the earlier part of the daf, where the man on the land showed a bill of sale.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Case facts: the holder privately admits the document is forged but claims a real one was lost.

steps.title: רבה believes him because he could have told a better lie
steps.stepSummary: רבה rules that the man on the land is believed, since he could have simply claimed the document was real.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Why would he lie? If he wanted to lie, he could have just said, 'It is a proper document.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives his ruling: we believe the man on the land about the lost real document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה's logic is the idea later called מיגו: the man had an easier claim available ('the document is real'), and he chose to admit it was fake. Someone making up a story would not hurt his own case like that, so his story about a lost real document is believable.

keyTerms.meaning: Why would he lie? He has no reason to make this up
The rule that a person is believed since he could have made a stronger claim

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a basic example of the מיגו idea, which shows up all over ש״ס.

phrases.english: Rabba said: Why would he lie?
If he wanted to, he could have said to him:
It is a proper document.
phrases.notes: He means: he could have just insisted the paper was real, and been believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules on the case set up in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The man on the land is believed, since he could have claimed the document was valid.

steps.title: רב יוסף objects that a forged document is worthless
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף asks רבה what he is relying on, since the document is admitted to be forged and is worth nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said to him: What are you relying on? On this document? This document is just a broken piece of pottery.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף challenges רבה's ruling, saying there is nothing real to base it on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף's point is that a מיגו needs something underneath it. Here the only evidence is a paper that everyone now agrees is fake. Without it, the man on the land has no proof at all, so the claim 'I could have lied' has nothing to support it.

keyTerms.meaning: A broken piece of pottery; something worthless

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said to him:
On what are you relying? On this document?
This document is just a broken piece of pottery.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יוֹסֵף: אַמַּאי סָמְכַתְּ
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's ruling that the man on the land is believed because of מה לו לשקר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The only evidence is admitted to be forged, so there is no real basis for the claim. The 'he could have lied' argument cannot stand on a worthless paper.
steps.whatToRemember: רבה: believe him, since he could have said the document was real. רב יוסף: a forged document is worthless, so there is nothing to rely on.

steps.title: A second case: a forged loan document
steps.stepSummary: A lender demands 100 זוז using a loan document. The borrower says it is forged, and the lender whispers to the judge that it is, but says he had a real one that got lost.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man said to another: 'Give me the hundred זוז you owe me, and here is the document.' The other said: 'It is forged.' The lender leaned over and whispered to the judge: 'Yes, it is forged. But I had a proper document, and it got lost. So I thought I would at least hold on to this one, whatever it is worth.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story that matches the first, this time about a loan instead of a field. It sets up the same argument again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The facts are the same as the first case, except here the person with the document is trying to collect money, not keep land he already holds. That difference matters, because in the first case the man was already living on the field, and here the lender wants to take money from someone else.

keyTerms.meaning: זוז coins, a type of money
That I am owed by you

phrases.english: There was a certain man who said to another:
Give me a hundred zuz
that you owe me, and here is the document.
He said to him: It is a forged document.
He leaned over and whispered to Rava:
phrases.notes: Notice the text says רבא here, yet the next line has רבה giving the ruling.

phrases.english: Yes, it is a forged document;
but I had a proper document,
and it got lost, and I said to myself:
I will hold this one in my hand, whatever it is worth.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַהוּא דְּאָמַר לְחַבְרֵיהּ: הַב לִי מְאָה זוּזִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story that matches step 1, but with a loan instead of land.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Case facts: a lender privately admits his loan document is forged but claims a real one was lost.

steps.title: רבה again believes him because he could have told a better lie
steps.stepSummary: רבה rules the same way in the loan case: the lender could have claimed the document was real, so he is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Why would he lie? If he wanted to lie, he could have just said, 'It is a proper document.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה applies his same reasoning to the loan case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה holds to his position even though here the lender is trying to collect money. For him, the fact that the lender admitted something that hurts his own case still makes him believable.

phrases.english: Rabba said: Why would he lie?
If he wanted to, he could have said to him:
It is a proper document.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules on the loan case from step 4, repeating רבה's reasoning from step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The lender is believed, since he could have claimed the document was valid.

steps.title: רב יוסף again objects that a forged document is worthless
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף gives the same objection: there is nothing to rely on, because the document is worthless.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said to him: What are you relying on? On this document? This document is just a broken piece of pottery.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף challenges רבה in the loan case exactly as he did in the land case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His point is the same: an admitted forgery proves nothing, so 'he could have lied' has nothing to rest on. In the loan case this is even sharper, since the lender wants to take money with no real evidence.

keyTerms.meaning: A small word showing an ongoing action ('are relying')

steps.whatToRemember: In both cases, land and loan, רבה believes the man because he could have said the document was real (מה לו לשקר). רב יוסף answers both times that an admitted forgery is worthless and cannot support the claim.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said to him:
On what are you relying? On this document?
This document is just a broken piece of pottery.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יוֹסֵף: אַמַּאי קָא סָמְכַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבה's ruling in step 5, the same way step 3 attacked step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's ruling that the lender is believed because of מה לו לשקר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The loan document is admitted to be forged, so it is worthless. The 'he could have lied' argument has no evidence to support it.

steps.title: Final ruling: follow רבה for land and רב יוסף for money
steps.stepSummary: רב אידי בר אבין rules that the הלכה follows רבה in the land case and רב יוסף in the money case, because in both cases whatever is already in place stays in place.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אידי בר אבין said: The הלכה follows רבה about land, and the הלכה follows רב יוסף about money. The הלכה follows רבה about land, meaning the land stays where it is. The הלכה follows רב יוסף about money, meaning the money stays where it is.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final ruling on the two cases it just discussed, the land case and the loan case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the land case, the man living on the land keeps it, as רבה said. In the loan case, the lender with the forged document collects nothing and the borrower keeps his money, as רב יוסף said. The idea that ties them together is that the court does not move property away from whoever already holds it.

keyTerms.meaning: The final law follows his opinion
Where it stands, let it stay

steps.whatToRemember: Land stays with the man holding it (like רבה), and money stays with the borrower (like רב יוסף). In both cases, the court leaves things where they are.
steps.confusionAlert: The two halves can look like they contradict each other. They do not, because the same idea runs through both: whoever is holding the property right now keeps it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling is the rule that אביי uses in the next steps to decide the guarantor case.

phrases.english: Rav Idi bar Avin said:
The halacha follows Rabba regarding land,
phrases.notes: This is the land case from steps 1 to 3, where the man on the land claimed he once had a real document.

phrases.english: and the halacha follows Rav Yosef regarding money.
The halacha follows Rabba regarding land,
meaning: where the land stands, let it stay.
phrases.notes: He means it stays with the person who is already living on it.

phrases.english: And the halacha follows Rav Yosef regarding money,
meaning: where the money stands, let it stay.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין: הִלְכְתָא כְּווֹתֵיהּ דְּרַבָּה בְּאַרְעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the dispute between רבה and רב יוסף from steps 2 to 6 by splitting the ruling between land and money.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Land stays with the man holding it, and money stays with the borrower.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה follows רבה for land and רב יוסף for money, because what is already in place stays in place.

steps.title: A guarantor demands money with a document the borrower says he already paid off
steps.stepSummary: A guarantor shows a document and demands 100 זוז from the borrower. The borrower says he already paid him, and the guarantor answers that the borrower later took the money back.
steps.simpleTranslation: A guarantor said to a borrower: Give me 100 זוז, because I paid the lender for you, and here is the document. The borrower said: Didn't I already pay you back? The guarantor said: Yes, but didn't you take the money back from me afterward?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new real-life case. It is setting up a question that will be sent to אביי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The guarantor admits that the borrower paid him back, so the document has already done its job and is now worth nothing. His only claim is that the borrower took the money back later, which is a new debt with no document behind it. This is just like the loan case, where the lender admitted his document was no good.

keyTerms.meaning: A guarantor (עָרֵב), who promises to pay the lender if the borrower does not

phrases.english: There was a certain guarantor who said to the borrower:
Give me one hundred zuz
that I paid the lender on your behalf,
and here is the document.
phrases.notes: This is the loan document the lender handed over to the guarantor once he was paid.

phrases.english: The borrower said to him: Didn't I pay you back?
He said: Didn't you then take it back from me?
phrases.notes: The guarantor admits he was paid. He is saying the borrower took the money back from him later.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new case that will test the ruling just given.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up a case: a guarantor holds a document that he admits was paid off, and he claims the money was taken back.

steps.title: רב אידי בר אבין asks אביי about the guarantor case
steps.stepSummary: רב אידי בר אבין sends the guarantor case to אביי and asks what the law is.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אידי בר אבין sent the question to אביי: In a case like this, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אידי בר אבין asks אביי how to rule in the guarantor case. This sets up אביי's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether the guarantor can collect. His document has already been paid off, and his claim of a new debt has no document of its own.

keyTerms.meaning: He sent it before him (sent the question)
In a case like this, what is the law?

phrases.english: Rav Idi bar Avin sent it
before Abaye:
In a case like this, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: שַׁלְחַהּ רַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּאַבָּיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the ruling on the case described in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can the guarantor collect when his document has been paid off and he claims the money was taken back?

steps.title: אביי answers: your own rule says the money stays where it is
steps.stepSummary: אביי is surprised by the question, because רב אידי בר אבין himself ruled that money stays where it is. So the borrower keeps the money.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי sent back: Why is he asking? He is the one who said the הלכה follows רבה about land and רב יוסף about money, meaning money stays where it is!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question using רב אידי בר אבין's own ruling from step 7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The guarantor case matches the loan case. In both, the document is admitted to be worth nothing, and the person demanding payment wants to collect on a claim the document does not prove. Since the הלכה follows רב יוסף for money, the borrower keeps his money and the guarantor collects nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: What is he asking? (the answer should be obvious)
Isn't he the one who said

steps.whatToRemember: A guarantor who admits he was paid cannot collect with that document by claiming the money was taken back. The money stays with the borrower.

phrases.english: Abaye sent him back:
What is he asking?
Isn't he the one who said:
phrases.notes: He means רב אידי בר אבין himself, in step 7.

phrases.english: the halacha follows Rabba regarding land,
and the halacha follows Rav Yosef regarding money,
meaning: where the money has been placed, let it stay!

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: מַאי תִּיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 9 by applying the rule from step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The money stays with the borrower, following רב יוסף's ruling about money.

steps.title: Limit: if the coins were returned because they were bad, the document still works
steps.stepSummary: אביי's ruling applies only when the guarantor says the borrower borrowed the money again. If the guarantor gave the coins back because they were worn or discolored, the document still has its full power.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only when he says to him: You later borrowed the money from me. But if he says: I gave the coins back to you because they were worn or discolored, then the document's power to collect is still in effect.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits the ruling it just gave. It explains when the guarantor loses and when he can still collect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the guarantor says the borrower borrowed the money again, that is a new loan with no document, so the old document is finished. But if he refused the coins because they were worn or discolored, the borrower never really paid. Then the original debt is still unpaid, and the document can still be used to collect.

keyTerms.meaning: The document's power to collect the debt (שעבוד)

steps.whatToRemember: A new loan cancels the old document. Bad coins that were handed back never counted as payment, so the old document still works.
steps.confusionAlert: In both versions the borrower got the coins back, so they can look the same. The difference is whether the first payment really counted. A new loan means it did, and coins given back for being bad mean it did not.

phrases.english: And this applies only where he says to him:
You then borrowed them from me.
But if he said to him:
I gave them back to you
because they were worn out or reddish,
phrases.notes: These are coins that people would not easily accept, so the guarantor never really took them as payment.

phrases.english: the lien of the document is still in effect.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָנֵי מִילֵּי, דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ: הֲדַרְתְּ אוֹזִפְתִּינְהוּ מִינַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits אביי's ruling to the case of a new loan, and gives an exception for coins that were refused.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the coins were handed back because they were bad, the original debt was never paid and the document can still be used to collect.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The guarantor loses only when he claims a new loan. If the payment was never real, the document keeps its power.

steps.title: A rumor about רבא בר שרשום and orphans' land
steps.stepSummary: A rumor spread that רבא בר שרשום was using land that belonged to orphans.
steps.simpleTranslation: People started saying that רבא בר שרשום was eating the produce of land that belonged to orphans.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new story. It is setting up a real case that will be clarified in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Using orphans' property without permission is a serious matter, so the rumor sounds bad. At this point we only know what people are saying, not what really happened.

keyTerms.meaning: Eating (profiting from) the produce of land

steps.confusionAlert: This is only a rumor. The story has not yet said that רבא בר שרשום did anything wrong.

phrases.aramaic: רָבָא בַּר שַׁרְשׁוּם נָפֵק עֲלֵיהּ קָלָא
phrases.english: About Rava bar Sharshom a rumor went out
that he was eating from land belonging to orphans.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא בַּר שַׁרְשׁוּם נָפֵק עֲלֵיהּ קָלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story after the גמרא's limit on the guarantor ruling in Step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A rumor claims רבא בר שרשום is profiting from orphans' land.

steps.title: אביי asks what really happened
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks רבא בר שרשום to explain the actual facts behind the rumor.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Tell me, my friend, what exactly happened?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי does not trust the rumor alone. He asks to hear the real facts, which sets up the explanation that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי wants the actual details of the case, not just what people are saying. The ruling will depend on exactly how the land came to רבא בר שרשום.

keyTerms.meaning: My friend (a warm way of speaking to someone)
The actual facts of the event

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: אֵימָא לִי אִיזִי,
phrases.english: Abaye said to him: Tell me, my friend,
the event itself, how was it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: אֵימָא לִי אִיזִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the rumor by asking for the true facts.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The real facts of how רבא בר שרשום came to be using the orphans' land.

steps.title: רבא בר שרשום explains he held the land as a pledge
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר שרשום begins explaining that he held the land as a משכנתא from the orphans' father.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I was holding the land as a משכנתא from the orphans' father, and I had...
steps.whatsHappening: רבא בר שרשום starts telling his side. He got the land legally as a pledge from the father, and his explanation continues in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This changes the picture: he did not just take orphans' land, he received it from their father as a משכנתא while the father was alive. The words 'and I had' show he is about to add another detail about what he was owed.

keyTerms.meaning: Land given to a lender as a pledge, where the lender may use its produce

phrases.english: He said to him: The land, as a pledge,
phrases.notes: A משכנתא is land given to a lender as security, and he gets to use its produce.

phrases.english: I was holding from the father of the orphans;
and I had

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַרְעָא בְּמַשְׁכַּנְתָּא הֲוָה נָקֵיטְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's question about the facts.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He held the land as a משכנתא from the orphans' father, and he had more to add.
